newsitem.title: USA: Dollar slides in slow trade ahead of European summit.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slides in slow trade ahead of European summit.

text.p: The dollar fell in slow trading Tuesday against most European currencies as nervousness over the direction of German interest rates set in ahead of a European nations summit this week.

Instigating the speculation was news that foreign policy experts from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's party were looking for ways to bind Italy into Europe's proposed monetary union while delaying its full entry.

This aided the mark against the dollar as the possibility of Italy not being a full-fledged member of the initial union in 1999 reduces the pressure on Germany to lower its interest rates, dealers said.

"I think people became less convinced this morning that the Bundesbank is going to ease rates to help form one European currency going into 1997," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.
"I think the market going into the summit is trading on rumours and expectations," he added.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the European Union, will host the bi-annual summit for member European nations this Friday and Saturday in Dublin.

The dollar closed down at 1.5530 marks from 1.5580 marks at Monday's close. Slow trading activity and little movement in exchange rates frustrated dealers, especially in comparison with the dollar's exciting tumble and recovery Friday on comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and U.S. November employment data.
"We've been in a real narrow dollar range today with not a lot of interest outside of the parameters of 1.5520 and 1.5560 marks," said Kevin Lawrie, global manager of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank.

The dollar jumped Tuesday after the mid-morning release of the National Association of Purchasing Management's latest semiannual survey, which showed most of its members see better U.S. economic growth in the first half of 1997 versus the second half of 1996.
"The only thing I noticed all day was NAPM caused a tick up in dollar trading," Lawrie said, lamenting a lack of market-moving news and data Tuesday.
However, the release of a record high U.S. current account trade deficit hurt the dollar, even though dealers said the data were of more interest to academics than traders.
The current account trade deficit was $47.96 billion in the third quarter, up 19 percent from the second quarter.
The dollar ended slightly lower against the yen, closing at 113.40 yen compared with 113.45 on Monday's close.

In overnight trade, the dollar eased off session highs against the yen amid talk that Kampo, the giant Japanese postal fund, would start hedging foreign bond risk. Such a move would likely entail the selling of dollars and European currencies for yen, dealers said.
In other trading, the dollar slipped to 1.3257 Swiss francs from 1.3283 at Monday's close but rose to Canadian $1.3578 from C$1.3553. Sterling rose to $1.6535 from $1.6470.
